clinicalPearls: A benign proliferative disorder in which the synovium undergoes cartilaginous metaplasia, forming multiple cartilage nodules that detach as loose bodies
Typically monoarticular, most often affecting the knee, followed by the hip, elbow and shoulder
Presents with joint pain, swelling, stiffness, crepitus and mechanical symptoms such as locking or catching from the loose bodies
When the loose bodies calcify or ossify they become visible on plain radiographs as multiple similarly sized calcified bodies within the joint
Non-mineralised cartilaginous bodies may be radiographically occult, so MRI is valuable to demonstrate them and the synovial disease
Diagnosis is confirmed histologically, and malignant transformation to synovial chondrosarcoma is rare but recognised
Treatment is surgical removal of loose bodies with synovectomy, and recurrence can occur if active synovial disease remains
reference.pathophysiology: Synovial chondromatosis is a benign neoplastic or metaplastic process in which the synovial membrane produces multiple foci of hyaline cartilage. These nodules enlarge, may calcify or ossify, and can detach from the synovium to become free-floating intra-articular loose bodies that continue to grow by drawing nutrition from the synovial fluid. Primary synovial chondromatosis arises de novo from the synovium and is now recognised to be a true clonal neoplastic process in many cases, whereas secondary chondromatosis develops from cartilage and bone fragments in a joint already damaged by osteoarthritis or trauma. The loose bodies mechanically damage articular cartilage and produce the locking, effusion and secondary degenerative change seen clinically.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary osteochondromatosis from osteoarthritis or trauma
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs showing multiple calcified intra-articular bodies of similar size
MRI to detect non-calcified cartilaginous bodies and characterise the synovial disease
CT to define ossified loose bodies and bony involvement
Ultrasound to demonstrate effusion and intra-articular bodies
Histological examination of resected tissue to confirm the diagnosis and exclude chondrosarcoma
redFlags: Rapid growth, aggressive bone destruction or a soft-tissue mass suggesting chondrosarcoma
Recurrent disease after surgery raising concern for persistent active or malignant synovium
Progressive joint destruction with severe mechanical impairment
Atypical extra-articular extension of the process
reference.prognosis: Primary synovial chondromatosis is benign and treatable with surgery, but recurrence is not uncommon when active synovium persists and untreated disease can cause secondary osteoarthritis; malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma is rare but carries a worse outlook.
pitfalls: Missing non-calcified cartilaginous loose bodies on plain radiographs and relying on them alone
Confusing it with pigmented villonodular synovitis on imaging
Failing to consider malignant transformation in aggressive or recurrent disease
Removing loose bodies without addressing the active synovium, leading to recurrence
references: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: Definitive treatment is surgical removal of the intra-articular loose bodies combined with synovectomy to remove the active synovium, performed arthroscopically or open
In secondary disease, manage the underlying joint pathology such as osteoarthritis that generated the cartilage fragments
Manage secondary degenerative change with analgesia and physiotherapy, and joint replacement for advanced arthritis
Monitor for recurrence, which is common when active synovium persists after incomplete synovectomy
Submit resected tissue for histological examination and remain alert to rare malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma
Refer to orthopaedic surgery, with rheumatology input as appropriate
